rationale: This replaces Pearson correlations with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariance matrices. The reference point is the Riemannian mean of the training fold's matrices. This was the strongest classic pipeline on ABIDE (Abraham 2017): it whitens each subject's connectome against the group geometry, which tends to reduce noise shared by the whole group and site/scanner effects while keeping individual differences. FC-region time series with zero signal get a unit diagonal so every matrix stays positive-definite. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

Scanner and protocol differences between ABIDE sites make each site's covariance matrices cluster around their own mean, and the scoring is done within each site. So I re-center each site's Ledoit-Wolf covariances on that site's Riemannian mean (C → M_s^{-1/2} C M_s^{-1/2}, which is Riemannian Procrustes re-centering) and then take the tangent space at the identity. This removes the site effect in the feature geometry before the linear classifier. The site means use no labels, which the brief allows for harmonization. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

I'm replacing the single CC200 model with an equal-weight ensemble over three parcellations: data-driven CC200 and CC400, plus anatomical AAL. Each atlas gets the same Ledoit-Wolf, per-site re-centering, tangent-space and logistic-regression pipeline as now. The atlases make partly independent errors from parcellation noise, and averaging across atlases was among the most reliable gains in Abraham 2017. Each atlas's L2 strength is scaled to its feature count, so its regularization stays comparable to the CC200 model that worked. I haven't run this, so its Dev score is unknown.

The multi-atlas ensemble timed out, so I'm going back to the single CC200 pipeline and adding one cheap harmonization step. Sites differ in timepoint count, TR and noise, so the spread of tangent vectors around each site's mean differs too, and re-centering alone doesn't fix that. The new step standardizes each tangent feature within each site, scaling it by the site's standard deviation pulled toward the pooled one. This is a ComBat-like, label-free version of the "stretch" step in Riemannian Procrustes analysis, and it puts every site's connectivity deviations on a common scale before the classifier. I haven't run it, so its Dev score is unknown.

Global signal regression (GSR) is the most disputed preprocessing choice in ABIDE. With GSR, connectivity estimates are less affected by motion and physiological noise, but the correlation structure gets shifted. That makes errors from the `filt_global` and `filt_noglobal` CC200 pipelines partly independent. I'm running the kept pipeline unchanged on both strategies and averaging the logit outputs from the two classifiers. It stays on CC200, so it should cost about 2× the current runtime, well below the CC400-driven timeout in round 3. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

I'm adding the anatomical AAL atlas (116 ROIs, including cerebellar parcels that matter in autism) as two more blocks, one per strategy (with and without GSR), using the same per-site re-centered tangent pipeline. Averaging across atlases was one of the most reliable gains in Abraham 2017, and AAL costs much less than the CC400 that timed out in round 3. The new blocks have fewer features, so each block's logistic-regression C is scaled to its feature count. Each block's logit is divided by the spread of its training-set logits before averaging, so blocks of different size get equal weight. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

L2 strength is currently fixed at C=0.001 for both the no-GSR and GSR blocks. The two strategies have different noise and correlation structure, so the best amount of shrinkage likely differs between them. I'll pick C separately for each block from a log grid, using grouped inner 5-fold CV on the training fold (grouped by `groups_train`). The selection criterion is within-site AUROC, the same metric the task is scored on, rather than a generic pooled score.

The two strategy blocks currently get equal weight in the average, even though GSR and no-GSR connectomes probably differ in how informative they are. This change reuses each block's inner-CV out-of-fold logits at its chosen C. It puts them on a common scale and picks simplex blend weights that maximize within-site AUROC, shrunk halfway toward equal weights to limit selection noise. Weaker blocks get down-weighted instead of diluting the ensemble, which is likely what hurt when AAL was added in round 6. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

Every block now uses z-scored series, so the model sees only connectivity and has no regional signal-amplitude or temporal-dynamics information. Atypical regional ALFF and BOLD dynamics are reported in autism. I'm adding a third, cheap block of per-ROI time-series features to the learned blend: relative log-amplitude (an ALFF proxy) and lag-1 autocorrelation, computed for both preprocessing strategies and z-scored within each site. The blend weights from round 8 can down-weight it if it turns out to be uninformative. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

Every block so far is static: it pools each scan into one connectome or one set of per-ROI statistics. Autism has been linked to atypical time-varying connectivity, meaning how much coupling between regions fluctuates during the scan, and that information is not in the current blocks. I'm adding one block of dynamic-connectivity features: for each pair of CC200 regions, the standard deviation across sliding windows of the Fisher-z correlation, computed on the no-GSR series only to limit runtime. These features are standardized within each site, because window statistics depend on the site's timepoint count and TR. The block gets its own grouped inner-CV logistic regression and goes into the existing learned blend, which can down-weight it if it adds nothing. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

I'm adding a fourth block of node-level graph features for each CC200 ROI under both strategies: signed connectivity strength (mean Fisher-z correlation to all other ROIs) and total coupling (mean squared correlation). Autism hypo/hyper-connectivity is often reported at the regional "global connectivity" level, and these low-dimensional summaries are hard for the L2 model on 20k edges to recover. The new block is site-standardized, gets its own grouped inner-CV logistic regression, and goes into the existing learned blend, which can down-weight it. It reuses the cached Ledoit-Wolf matrices, so it adds little runtime. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

I'm adding time-series cropping augmentation to the connectivity blocks. For each subject and strategy, I compute a Ledoit-Wolf correlation matrix on each half of the scan. The two halves go into training as extra copies with the subject's label and weight 0.5, so each subject's samples share one CV group. They use the same per-site re-centering and standardization as the full-scan matrices. With p >> n and short, noisy scans, this should teach the L2 classifier to ignore edges that are unstable within a subject. Test subjects are still scored on their full-scan connectome. To save memory, the two half matrices for each subject are stored in one array, one in the upper triangle and one in the lower.

People with autism show shorter intrinsic neural timescales, meaning faster decay of BOLD autocorrelation, especially in sensory and unimodal regions (Watanabe 2019). The ALFF/autocorrelation block is the only thing that has helped since round 8, but it uses lag-1 only. So I'm adding per-ROI lag-2 and lag-3 autocorrelations for both strategies to that same block, without creating a new blend block. Together the lags describe the autocorrelation decay curve that defines the timescale. Site standardization already absorbs the different TRs across sites.

Every connectivity block so far comes from the one data-driven CC200 parcellation. Parcellation noise is a major error source in ABIDE, so averaging across atlases should help (Abraham 2017). Earlier attempts failed for other reasons: CC400 hit the time limit, and AAL was mixed in with equal weights before the blend weights were learned. This round adds one cheap, functionally defined Dosenbach-160 block (no-GSR only, about 12.9k tangent features, cerebellar ROIs included). It goes through the same per-site re-centered tangent pipeline, gets its own inner-CV C, and enters the existing learned blend, which can down-weight it if it doesn't help.

Some subjects have all-zero, out-of-field-of-view ROIs. Right now those ROIs are filled with an uncorrelated unit row, plus a lag-1 autocorrelation of 0 and a relative amplitude of 0. After per-site whitening, each subject with a dead ROI becomes an outlier: the decoupled row spreads into the subject's live edges, and a 0 autocorrelation sits far below the usual ~0.6–0.9. That outlier can push the subject's score around within its site. This round fills each dead ROI's covariance with the Gaussian conditional estimate from the subject's live ROIs and its site's mean connectome, which keeps the matrix positive-definite. Dead-ROI features are then treated as missing in the per-site standardization and set to the site mean, in both the tangent and time-series blocks. When no subject has a dead ROI, the pipeline gives exactly the same result as before. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

Within-site AUROC ignores any constant offset per site. But the per-site centering subtracts the site mean, which depends on the site's ASD/TD ratio. As a result, in an imbalanced site both classes are shifted along the very direction that separates them, which blurs the pooled training signal. This change re-centers each training site on the midpoint of its two class means, using training labels only, inside every inner and outer fit. Test-time offsets don't change within-site rankings, so test data needs no labels. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

I'm adding a regional-homogeneity proxy to the existing time-series block instead of creating a new blend block, since every new block so far (rounds 10, 11, 14) has lowered the score. Each CC400 ROI is mapped, without labels, to its parent CC200 parcel using the group-mean CC400×CC200 correlation. The new feature is the Fisher-z correlation between each CC400 sub-region and its parent parcel. It measures how coherent each parcel is internally, which tests the reduced local connectivity / ReHo reported in autism. None of the current blocks captures this: they only have connectivity between parcels plus amplitude and autocorrelation. I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

I'm adding subject-level reliability weighting, which is new to this history. For each subject and strategy, I fit a Ledoit-Wolf correlation matrix to each half of the scan and measure the affine-invariant Riemannian distance between the two. A large distance means a noisy connectome (motion, short or non-stationary scans). Each training subject's logistic loss is down-weighted by that distance relative to its site's median, which is computed without labels. Test subjects are scored exactly as before. The hypothesis is that unreliable training connectomes are mostly noise in the p >> n fit, so trusting them less should sharpen the weight vector. This is a soft version of the motion exclusion many ABIDE studies use, and it removes no subjects.

For short scans with T ≲ p, Ledoit-Wolf shrinks toward a scaled identity, which distorts every subject's connectome in the same blind way. I'm switching to a PoSCE-style population prior (Rahim et al. 2019). Each subject's empirical correlation matrix is shrunk toward its own site's mean correlation matrix, using a label-free Ledoit-Wolf-type weight α = (estimated sampling variance of the subject's edges) / ‖S − site mean‖². Noisy or short scans get pulled toward the site mean more, and real individual structure is kept. The rest of the pipeline (re-centering, tangent space, standardization, blend) stays the same.
